_meta.note: The 8 Jev rubric categories, one Jev `score` question each. This file is the source of truth (scripts/jev-gate is self-contained in CI). Instructions describe ONLY what to score and the level criteria — say NOTHING about confidence: confidence is the model's own axis (its certainty in the verdict), so the rubric must never instruct, calibrate, or nudge it; a low-confidence score already routes to human sign-off. Duplication was dropped 2026-09-19 — it needs cross-file context the per-file gate cannot supply, so its scores were never decidable.
_meta.authoring: Jev returns a probability per level; `score` is the mean of that distribution and `confidence` is how peaked it is. A rubric earns high confidence when a reader could settle on ONE level from this file alone. Rules measured on this repo (2026-09-20): (1) one dimension per question — a level that is an OR-list of unrelated defects spreads the distribution; (2) open with 'Look only at X' and name the observable thing; (3) settle every definitional edge in a 'these do NOT count' list (log-and-continue is not swallowing, argument arrays are not injection); (4) do not let one ambiguous find drop a file from level 4 to level 0 — that yields a bimodal 0-vs-4 split and a meaningless mean; reserve such cliffs for finds that are unmistakable when present; (5) put role handling (test/fixture/mock/story/type rate 4) in the level-4 criterion as well as the instructions, never as an opening clause; (6) ask nothing that needs another file (whether an import exists, whether a caller catches); (7) avoid numeric thresholds — Jev counts badly.
_meta.scale: Every question is a Jev `score`. Levels run 0 (worst) to 4 (best). Higher always means healthier code, so the overall score is a plain mean.

code_smells.instructions: Rate this source code for Martin Fowler-style code smells that are OBSERVABLE IN THIS FILE ALONE — each file is judged independently, so do not consider smells that require seeing other files. In scope: long methods, large classes, primitive obsession, data clumps, long parameter lists, speculative generality, and boolean/flag parameters that silently switch a function's behavior (control coupling) — a pattern easy to accumulate in TypeScript because optional booleans are cheap to add. Do NOT judge cross-file smells you cannot see from a single file, such as shotgun surgery (one change rippling across many files) or feature envy (a method more interested in another class not shown here). Higher means fewer, less harmful smells.
criteria: Riddled with smells: bloated methods and classes, primitive obsession, data clumps, long parameter lists, and/or flag-parameter control coupling throughout
Frequent smells that clearly hurt readability and make change unsafe
Some smells present but localized and low impact
Mostly clean; only minor, defensible smells remain
No meaningful code smells; cohesive and well factored

security.instructions: Look only for these constructs written in this file: a literal credential, API key, private key, or crypto key/IV in non-test code; Math.random or a fast hash (MD5/SHA-1) used for a token, session id, nonce, salt, password or signature; a shell command STRING built from variables, or a subprocess spawned with `shell: true`; a SQL/NoSQL query STRING built by concatenating variables; eval/new Function on a non-literal; innerHTML/dangerouslySetInnerHTML set from a variable; a filesystem path built by inserting an id, name or other string variable into a path segment or filename with no check in this file that confines it (no allowlist, pattern test, basename, or startsWith(root) check); TLS/certificate verification disabled; a server-side request handler or middleware whose auth/permission check allows the request when the check errors or a value is missing. These do NOT count: argument arrays passed to spawn/execFile without a shell; parameterized or ORM-built queries; path.join/resolve of constants, configured roots, or values checked in this file; logging error messages; environment-variable lookups; client-side UI state; placeholder or dummy values; Math.random for jitter, sampling or UI. Do not speculate about callers or where inputs come from. Rate what is written here. Test, fixture, mock, story and type files rate 4.
criteria: Several of the listed constructs, or one that is unmistakable and severe (real-looking secret, interpolated shell string, fail-open server auth)
One of the listed constructs is clearly present
A borderline case: something resembling a listed construct, with partial validation or escaping in this file
Relevant sinks exist (subprocess, query, HTML, crypto) but every use here is the safe form
None of the listed constructs, and no relevant sinks, appear in this file — or the file is itself a test, fixture, mock, story or type declaration

complexity_clean_code.instructions: Rate this source code for complexity and Robert C. Martin clean-code qualities: function size and single responsibility, name clarity, and complexity as a reader would actually feel it. Judge complexity qualitatively, not by literal branch counting (exact counting is a known weak spot for this model). Prefer a cognitive-complexity lens over a cyclomatic one: nested control flow that forces a reader to hold multiple contexts at once (for example a loop containing a try/catch containing a conditional) is worse than the same number of sequential, early-return guard clauses, even when both have a similar number of branches. Higher means simpler and cleaner.
criteria: Very hard to follow: deeply nested control flow that forces holding multiple contexts at once, huge functions, unclear names
Often complex or poorly named; frequent cognitive overload from nesting or mixed concerns, even where individual branch counts look modest
Moderate complexity; some nesting or nested error handling that could flatten into guard clauses, several functions or names could be simpler
Mostly simple and well named; small focused functions with shallow, mostly linear control flow
Clean and simple: small single-purpose functions, clear names, shallow linear control flow with no nested-context reading burden

comments.instructions: Look only at the comments in this file. A bad comment is one of: a comment that restates what the next line of code plainly does; a banner or divider comment; commented-out code; a lint or type suppression (eslint-disable, oxlint-disable, @ts-ignore, @ts-expect-error) with no specific reason given; a comment that apologizes for or preaches about a workaround instead of stating the constraint. Every other comment (explaining why, documenting an API contract, a suppression that names its specific reason) is fine. Rate how many bad comments the file contains.
criteria: Bad comments throughout the file
Many bad comments
A few bad comments
One or two bad comments
No bad comments, or no comments at all

testability.instructions: Look only at what this file's logic touches DIRECTLY: the filesystem (node:fs), child processes, network (fetch/http), process.env/argv/exit, the clock (Date.now, new Date() used in logic), timers, Math.random, browser globals (window, document, localStorage), and module-level mutable state (a top-level `let`, or a top-level Map/Set/array/object mutated by functions). Rate how entangled the logic is with these. It is NOT entangled when such a dependency arrives as a parameter, constructor argument, options field, prop or context — including a parameter with a production default. Calls to imported project functions are out of scope: you cannot see what they do. Files that are only types, constants, data, JSX markup or pure functions are not entangled. A test, fixture, mock/stub, story, or type-declaration file (judge from its path, the state's `role_hint` if present, and its content) has no logic of its own to unit test: rate it 4 regardless of what it touches.
criteria: Nearly all logic directly touches ambient I/O, globals or module-level mutable state, with no way to substitute them
Most logic directly touches them
Some logic directly touches them; the rest is pure or parameterized
Only a thin edge touches them directly (an entry point or default argument); the logic is pure or parameterized
Nothing touches them directly: pure logic, injected dependencies, or no logic at all — or the file is itself a test, fixture, mock, story or type declaration

error_handling.instructions: Look only at catch blocks, .catch() handlers, and un-awaited promises in this file. Rate how often a failure is silently lost. A failure is SILENTLY LOST when a catch is empty, or discards the error and continues or returns a default/success-shaped value with no log, report, rethrow, or comment explaining why ignoring is safe; or when a promise is neither awaited, returned, nor given a rejection handler. A failure is NOT lost when the catch logs, reports, rethrows, converts the error into a typed result, or documents a deliberate best-effort ignore; nor when an error simply propagates to the caller. Unvalidated parameters are out of scope. A test, fixture, mock/stub, story, or type-declaration file (judge from its path, the state's `role_hint` if present, and its content) has no failure path of its own: rate it 4.
criteria: Most catches in this file silently lose the failure
Several places silently lose a failure
One place silently loses a failure
Catches handle or propagate errors; at most a documented, deliberate ignore
No failure is silently lost, or the file has no catch blocks and no promises — or the file is itself a test, fixture, mock, story or type declaration

concurrency_and_idempotency.instructions: Rate this source code for event-loop discipline and idempotency under retries and partial failure. A background loop, periodic poll, reconcile pass, boot sweep, or fill job that iterates a collection whose size grows with the database or workload MUST chunk its synchronous work and yield the event loop between chunks (e.g. via a yield helper) — a tight synchronous loop over an unbounded or growing collection on the shared Node event loop is a critical violation, since it can freeze every other request the process serves. Commands, lifecycle steps, and processing loops must also be idempotent: they should converge to the same end state whether run once or replayed after a crash, restart, or retry, with no double-application of a side effect (e.g. double-charging, double-inserting, re-sending a notification) on a retried attempt. A retry loop or subprocess-spawn loop with no upper bound is also a smell here. First judge the file's role from its path, the state's `role_hint` (if present), and its content: MOST files have no background loop, no shared-state mutation, and no retryable command — pure functions, types, UI components, tests, fixtures, mocks, stories, and config have no such surface at all. Score these near the top (4) by default; do not penalize a file for lacking yield points or idempotency guards it was never meant to have. Apply the full bar only to code that actually runs a loop over a growing collection, a periodic or background job, or a retryable command or lifecycle step.
criteria: Has a background loop, poll, reconcile pass, or retry/spawn loop that is a critical risk: a tight synchronous loop over an unbounded/growing collection with no yield, or a side effect that clearly double-applies on retry
Same surface present but only partially mitigated: yields are missing on some paths, or idempotency holds for the common case but breaks under a plausible crash or retry
Has the surface and mostly handles it correctly, but a genuine gap remains (e.g. an unbounded retry with no cap, or a lifecycle step whose idempotency is unclear)
Has the surface and handles it correctly; only a minor, defensible gap remains
No background loop, retryable command, or shared-state mutation to worry about — or, where present, it chunks/yields correctly and converges to the same end state under crash, restart, or retry

ai_slop.instructions: Rate this file for tells of unedited LLM-agent output visible in the file's own code and comments. Tells: assistant chatter or first-person change narration in a comment ('Here is the updated function', 'I've refactored this', 'this is a simplified version', 'in a real app you would'); near-identical helpers with different names doing the same job; an interface, strategy or config knob with a single implementation justified only 'for future use'; try/catch around code that cannot throw, or the same guard repeated verbatim many times; placeholder names (data2, temp, foo, item1); a TODO describing work the code already does, or a stub left unimplemented; comments narrating nearly every line. These are NOT tells: text inside string literals, fixtures or test data; plain, terse or unremarkable code; doc comments; long explanatory why-comments; whether imports or APIs exist (that needs other files). A generated file, fixture, mock, type declaration, or plain data file has no authorial voice to judge: rate it 4.
criteria: Assistant chatter or first-person change narration is left in a comment
Several different tells appear repeatedly
One clear tell appears
One faint, arguable tell
No tell is present — or the file is generated, a fixture, a mock, a type declaration or plain data
